name: Cheekbone makeup contour/highlight

card.summary: Shading and highlighting to imitate defined cheekbones; reversible and low-risk, with no clinical research behind it.
card.note: Effect is visual and depends on lighting and application.

quick.overview:
Cheekbone contouring uses darker and lighter makeup to suggest more defined cheekbones.

It is a styling technique and has not been studied clinically.
quick.mechanism: Shading under the cheekbone and highlighting on top change the perceived depth and shape of the cheek through light and shadow.
quick.risks: Makeup carries the usual risks of skin irritation or allergic reaction with some products. The effect is temporary and washes off.

lead: Cheekbone contouring and highlighting is a makeup technique that creates the look of higher, sharper cheekbones. A shade one or two tones darker than the skin goes in the hollow beneath the cheekbone, and a lighter or shimmery highlighter goes on the raised top of the bone, so that the shadow recedes and the highlight catches light [1]. It lets people change how their face reads in photos and in person without surgery, and it washes off the same day.

The method sits within the broader practice of contouring, which also shades the sides of the nose, the temples and the jawline [1]. Wikipedia traces it from Elizabethan stage makeup and 1930s Hollywood work by Max Factor through Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book Face Forward to the intense, widely shared looks of the 2010s popularised by Kim Kardashian and other makeup artists [1][4][5].

In appearance communities it is discussed as a reversible way to add facial definition, for people who want more prominent cheekbones, a leaner midface or a stronger photographic presence. No clinical research has measured how contour makeup changes perceived attractiveness.

chain: Darker shade under the cheekbone, lighter shade on top
Shadow and highlight change how the cheek reflects light
Cheekbones look higher and the midface looks more defined
angle.text: Contour and highlight change how light falls across the cheek, so the cheekbone looks more prominent and the face looks leaner or more sculpted. The effect depends on shade match, blending and lighting, and it lasts until the makeup is removed.

infobox: Powder, cream or stick contour and highlighter
Hollow beneath the cheekbone; apple and top of the cheekbone
Max Factor (1930s), Kevyn Aucoin (1990s-2000), social media (2010s)

paras: Wikipedia describes contouring as using cosmetics to define and sculpt facial structure: a tone one or two shades darker than the skin goes into hollows of the cheeks, along the sides of the nose and at the temples to create shadow and a slimming look, while a tone one or two shades lighter goes on prominent areas such as the apples of the cheeks, the tip of the nose and the forehead, nose and chin [1]. For cheekbones, the dark shade goes below the bone and the highlight sits on the raised area above it [1].
Shadow tends to recede and light tends to advance, which is why placement along the hollow and on the bone changes how the cheek appears, and why the result varies with lighting and camera angle.

Powder contour products are usually sold in palettes with light and dark shades, while cream products give a more emphasised, intense look [1]. Strobing is a lighter-only variation that uses light-reflecting products with little or no dark shading, so the cheekbone is brought forward by shine rather than shadow [1]. Beauty brands began selling dedicated contour and strobing products in the 2010s, moving the technique from celebrity makeup artists to affordable ranges [1].

Wikipedia records that Elizabethan actors used chalk and soot so audiences could read expressions, and that greasepaint replaced soot once electric stage lighting arrived in the late 1800s [1]. In the 1920s and 1930s film actress Marlene Dietrich was noted for contouring her face to emphasise its natural lines [1].

Max Factor Sr., a Polish-born makeup artist who settled in Los Angeles in 1904, built much of his reputation on makeup designed for film, including a flexible cream greasepaint around 1914, makeup for black-and-white film in 1928 and the Pan-Cake matte base of the late 1930s for Technicolor [5]. Wikipedia's contouring article adds that in 1934 he introduced shading so faces would not look flat on screen, and in 1945 presented a tutorial on contouring for different face shapes [1]. Actresses of the 1950s such as Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe and Elizabeth Taylor wore subtler forms of shading [1].

Kevyn Aucoin, a self-taught American makeup artist who moved to New York in the early 1980s and whose clients included Madonna, Whitney Houston and Jennifer Lopez, published Face Forward in 2000; it is credited with introducing makeup sculpting and contouring to the general public [4][1]. In the 2010s Kim Kardashian and other makeup artists made strong contour looks mainstream, and the technique spread through social media, which Wikipedia also credits with popularising 'body contouring' on areas such as shins and breasts from the 2000s [1].

The apparent shape of the cheek reflects both the skeleton and the soft tissue over it. Surgical anatomy papers describe the midcheek as built from lid-cheek, malar and nasolabial segments over the midcheek skeleton [2], and describe age-related changes in separate superficial and deep fat compartments [3]. Those papers concern surgery and injectables rather than makeup, but they describe the structures that contour and highlight imitate: a prominent malar bone with a hollow beneath it.

Contouring is used in everyday makeup, on stage and screen, and by drag performers, who use it to emphasise or soften features [1]. In appearance and grooming circles it is discussed as a non-surgical, low-cost way for people who want stronger cheekbones, a leaner midface or a sharper look in photographs, alongside facial-fat reduction, fillers and implants for those who prefer lasting changes. Users on forums describe it as a way to preview how a more defined midface would look before committing to a procedure.

Related approaches include highlighter-only strobing [1], nose and jaw contouring [1], and the non-makeup routes to more defined cheeks that appearance communities discuss: reducing facial fat, filler in the malar area and cheek implants. Anatomy literature on fat compartments and midcheek structure underlies the surgical and injectable versions [2][3].
No studies found. Anatomy literature describes the cheek but does not examine contour makeup.

timeline.event: Max Factor Sr. emigrates to Los Angeles and begins supplying theatrical makeup to the film industry.[5]
Max Factor develops a thinner cream greasepaint suited to motion pictures.[5]
Max Factor Sr. adds shading so faces do not look flat on screen.[1]
Max Factor presents a tutorial on contouring for different face shapes.[1]
A Vogue cover with Cindy Crawford boosts Kevyn Aucoin's career.[4]
Kevyn Aucoin publishes Face Forward, credited with introducing contouring to the public.[4][1]
Celebrity makeup artists, social media and dedicated contour and strobing products make strong contouring mainstream.[1]
